## Teaching approach

The seminar runs in five parts. **Part 1** rebuilds Rohrer's DAG vocabulary through one running example—whether attending a selective college pays off—with interactive confounder, collider, and mediator paths; it adds a verbal explanation of why conditioning on a collider induces dependence and places mediation and moderation beside the DAG concepts. Advanced transfer exercises remain hidden as optional backup slides. **Part 2** moves from DAGs to experimental design: the Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference, scientific versus statistical solutions, Druckman's 2×2 typology, the assumptions behind randomization, the different jobs of assignment, sampling, and sample size, experimental types and goals, realism, treatment validity, the four validity questions, and a qualified external-validity argument based on effect heterogeneity and moderator coverage. **Part 3** is a full live deep-dive on Correll, Benard, and Paik (2007): students distinguish the population wage-gap puzzle from the randomized parental-status-cue estimand, propose the design, inspect the lab and field-audit procedures, and critique what each identifies. **Part 4** repeats the structure for Craig and Richeson (2014/2015), explicitly separating actual demographic change from randomized message exposure, calibrating the corrected Study 1 evidence, and comparing measured mediation with Studies 3a/3b's experimental manipulation of the proposed status-threat mechanism. **Part 5** synthesizes both cases and closes with a project application and exit question.

## Source conventions

Almost every DAG in Part 1 (the college-and-income chain/fork/collider/combined DAGs, the two "harder version" stretch DAGs, and the social-media capstone DAG) is drawn live by the scored interactive widget in `open-closed-simulation.html`, not a static image — the only static DAG still reused from Week 10 is Rohrer's own Figure 3 (genetic confounding), copied from `week-10/assets/`. New static DAGs for this week (the naive motherhood DAG, the statistical-vs-status-discrimination comparison, the randomized-design DAG, the three candidate DAGs for the racial-shift case, the full status-threat/assuaged-threat DAG, the mediation-vs-moderation pair, and the independence/SUTVA/exclusion-restriction violation DAGs) are generated by `make-figures.py`. Tables and figures from the three readings (Druckman's Tables 2.3/3.1; Correll, Benard, and Paik's Tables 1 and 6; Craig and Richeson's Figure 1 and Tables 2–3) are cropped directly from the source PDFs and credited on their slides. Slide numbers include the automatic title slide.

## Slide-by-slide script

### Slide 2: Questions for today

**Talk track**

Today we are moving from causal diagrams to experimental design. We will begin by deciding which paths should be open or closed, then ask how an intervention can close a path by design. The two papers at the end let us see that logic operating in published research.

**Teaching detail**

Walk through the five parts at a high level. Tell students Parts 3 and 4 will look different from a typical lecture: before every design reveal, you will ask them to propose the design themselves, and before every results reveal, you will ask them to critique the design. Readings for today: Druckman (2023), chapters 2–3; Correll, Benard, and Paik (2007); Craig and Richeson (2014, with the 2015 correction).

### Slide 3: Running example: does a selective college pay off?

**Talk track**

Start with a familiar correlation: people who attend more selective colleges tend to earn more. Our task is not to decide immediately that college caused the difference. Our task is to list the different causal structures that could produce the same observed relationship.

**Ask students**

What are three different reasons this correlation might appear?

**Teaching detail**

Set up the single running example before showing any vocabulary at all. The correlation itself is uncontroversial and genuinely documented (this is the real empirical debate behind Dale and Krueger's work, which Week 10 already touched on); what's contested is what produces it. Tell students: rather than hopping between a new topic for every structure, we are going to answer "what's going on here?" three different ways, one at a time, with the same two boxes — attending a selective college, and income — on screen the whole time. We'll save the "why/how does it work" story for last, after we've dealt with whether the relationship is even real.

### Slide 4: Open or closed? Through family SES and ability

**Talk track**

Our first explanation is confounding. Family resources and prior ability can affect both college attendance and later income. If that is the whole story, selective college and income move together even if the college itself has no effect.

**Ask students**

Before clicking anything, is this path open or closed? What variable would you condition on?

**Teaching detail**

First candidate explanation, and the one to deal with before anything else: is this relationship even real, or might it be entirely spurious? This is a **confounding** story: Family SES & ability → attending a selective college, and Family SES & ability → income, with no requirement that the college itself does anything at all. If this is the whole story, the correlation is two symptoms of the same underlying cause, not cause and effect.

Point out the dotted gray line first, before anything else: it runs straight from "attends a selective college" to income in every widget today, labeled "the relationship we want to identify." It's deliberately dotted, not solid — we don't yet know whether it's causal, confounded, or an artifact, which is exactly the question each widget is built to answer. It always "completes the trip" when you hit Play, because it isn't a path that can be blocked; it's a reminder of what every other path underneath it is trying to explain.

First widget pass. Uncontrolled, hit Play: the dot travels from "attends a selective college" back through Family SES & ability and on to income — open, and this is **bias**, not a real effect, because the "path" runs backward through a common cause rather than forward through a mechanism. Click the node to control for it, then Play again: the dot now stops. Controlling for a true confounder is the one case, of the three stories we'll see today, where "control for it" is unambiguously the right move. Name it: this structure is a **fork**, and the middle node is a **confounder**. Even after controlling for this, the relationship might still be fully explained away by something else — one more trap before we get to ask "why."

### Slide 5: Selection can create a relationship

**Talk track**

Now imagine that college and income are unrelated in the full population, but the dataset is assembled using either of two selection routes. Selection is now a common effect of college status and income. That common effect is the collider.

**Ask students**

If a person is not from a selective college but appears in this dataset, what must be true about the other selection route?

**Teaching detail**

Second candidate explanation, and the one students find least intuitive. Use this as a deliberately mechanical example, not as a factual claim about how alumni surveys normally work. College status and income could be independent in the full population. But the dataset is assembled from either of two sources: one selected on college status and one selected on income. Being included is therefore a common effect of college status and income — a collider.

The earlier alumni-office story was ambiguous because being contacted, responding, and being observed are different events. Here the selection rule is explicit: a person enters the analytic dataset if they are on either list. The arrows into inclusion describe that rule directly.

### Slide 6: Open or closed? Analyzing only the recruited sample

**Talk track**

Before we select anyone, the two arrows meet at inclusion and the path is closed. Once we restrict the analysis to included people, knowing how someone did not enter tells us more about how they must have entered. The two causes become informative about one another.

**Teaching detail**

Second widget pass. "Attends a selective college" and income both point *into* "Included in dataset." In the full population, hit Play: the two arrows meet and stop at inclusion. One cause tells us nothing about the other. Now click the inclusion node — meaning "analyze only recruited people" — and Play again. The path becomes statistically active because learning that one selection route was absent makes the other route more likely. The next slide shows this with counts.

Name it: inclusion is a **collider**. Restricting the analysis to selected cases can create an association that was absent in the full population.

### Slide 7: The numbers make the collider visible

**Talk track**

The missing lower-right cell is the whole argument. Nonselective, lower-income people are absent. Inside the selected sample, a person from a nonselective college must have entered through the high-income list, so college status predicts income even though it did not in the population.

**Ask students**

What changed between the population table and the selected sample: the causal effect, or who is observed?

**Teaching detail**

Walk through the missing lower-right cell. In the full population, college selectivity and income are independent: half of each college group has high income. The selection rule deletes only nonselective, lower-income people. Inside the selected sample, learning that someone did not attend a selective college tells us they must have entered through the high-income list. College status therefore predicts income even though it did not in the population.

This induced dependence is what it means for X → S ← Y to become statistically active when we condition on S. The arrows do not reverse. Also be precise with terminology: this is an opened **noncausal path** and selection bias; it is not literally a back-door path, because a back-door path must begin with an arrow into X.

Use a simple diagnostic sentence: **when you know the outcome happened, its possible causes begin to explain one another.** The same logic drives Berkson's paradox among hospital patients, admissions bias among students selected on either grades or athletics, and publication bias when both rigor and novelty affect whether a study is published.

Do not say the arrows literally reverse. The causal arrows remain pointed into the collider. What changes is the statistical information flow: after conditioning on the common effect, observing one cause provides information about the other.

We've now dealt with "is it spurious?" and "is it a trap in how the sample was built?" Suppose neither applies, and the relationship really is real. Last question: *why*?

### Slide 8: If the effect is real, what carries it?

**Talk track**

Suppose the relationship survives our concerns about confounding and selection. We can now ask a different question: what carries the effect from college to income? A professional network is one possible mediator.

**Teaching detail**

Third candidate explanation, and deliberately last, because it only makes sense to ask *how* something works once you've asked *whether* it's real. This is a **mediation** story: attending a selective college → professional network → income. If true, part or all of the apparent effect is real, just not direct — it works *through* the network.

### Slide 9: Open or closed? Through professional network

**Talk track**

Here the path through the network is part of the effect we are trying to understand. If we control for the network, we stop that part of the effect. This is why controlling for every available variable is not a safe general rule.

**Ask students**

If our goal is the total effect of college, should we control for professional network? Why or why not?

**Teaching detail**

Third widget pass. Leave the network uncontrolled and hit Play: the mediator's own dot travels all the way from "attends a selective college" to income, pulsing green — if this story is true, that is the real effect, flowing through the mechanism. Now click the node to control for it, and Play again: the dot stops dead at Professional network with a red block mark. This is **overcontrol** — holding network quality fixed compares people with equally strong networks, which removes exactly the part of the effect this story says is real. Name the vocabulary once, lightly: this middle node is called a **mediator**, and the structure is a **chain**. This is also the one story, of the three, that answers *why* rather than *whether* — which is exactly why it had to come last.

### Slide 10: The same three nodes can play different roles

**Talk track**

These three structures look similar because each has three nodes, but the middle node plays a different role. A confounder creates a noncausal association, a collider blocks a path until we condition on it, and a mediator carries a causal effect.

**Ask students**

For each row, does controlling for the middle variable remove bias, create bias, or remove part of the effect?

**Teaching detail**

Now that students have seen all three stories concretely, generalize to the vocabulary and the general X/M/Y notation other papers will use. This table is the payoff of going through the college-and-income example three times, in the order we actually reasoned through it — is it spurious, is it a sampling trap, and only then, why — rather than introducing fork/collider/chain as three arbitrary labels up front. Every DAG we draw for the rest of the session is one of these three rows, however many times it's duplicated or nested.

### Slide 11: A mediator explains how an effect travels

**Talk track**

Mediation asks how an effect travels. The total effect includes the path through the mediator and any path that bypasses it. If our target is the total effect, controlling for the mediator removes part of what we are trying to estimate.

**Teaching detail**

Name mediation here, at the moment students first understand a chain, rather than postponing the term until the middle of the experiment lecture. A mediator answers a mechanism question: how does X change Y? The professional-network example is mediation because the proposed effect of college selectivity travels through network formation.

Distinguish the estimands. The total effect includes the mediated path plus any direct path. Conditioning on M removes the path through M, so it cannot estimate the total effect. It may be tempting to call the remaining coefficient the direct effect, but the same warning from Rohrer still applies: unless the mediator itself is randomized or all mediator–outcome confounding is blocked, that direct/indirect decomposition is not automatically causal. Correll will measure proposed mediators; Craig and Richeson will later manipulate one.

### Slide 12: The effect may differ across groups

**Talk track**

Moderation is a different question. We are no longer asking how the effect travels; we are asking whether the effect is larger, smaller, or reversed for different kinds of people. Here the proposed moderator is family SES before college.

**Ask students**

Why might selective college matter more for students from lower-SES families? What result would count as moderation?

**Teaching detail**

Place moderation directly after mediation so students can contrast two different questions while the DAG vocabulary is active. Mediation asks how the effect travels. Moderation asks whether the size or direction of the effect differs across values of a pre-treatment variable.

Use the same running example. The moderation hypothesis is that selective college provides a larger income benefit for students from lower-SES families because it supplies networks and institutional access they were less likely to have already. For students from higher-SES families, the marginal benefit may be smaller because some of those resources were already available. This is an illustrative hypothesis, not a numerical claim about the size of the real effect.

Point out an important complication: pre-college family SES can be both a **confounder** and a **moderator**. It may predict who attends a selective college and adult income, while also changing the treatment effect. Those are separate roles. Identification still requires closing the back door through SES; moderation is then assessed by comparing the identified college effect across SES levels, often with a treatment × SES interaction.

### Slide 13: A back door begins by pointing into the treatment

**Talk track**

A back-door path begins by pointing into the treatment. To identify a total effect, we close those paths without blocking the causal paths that carry the treatment effect and without opening colliders.

**Teaching detail**

One-slide restatement, no new content. This sets up the combined widget next, where students need the formal rule because more than one structure is in play at once and intuition alone starts to fail.

### Slide 14: One DAG can contain all three structures

**Talk track**

This diagram combines everything we have just separated. Family SES is a confounder, professional network is a mediator, and inclusion is a collider. The correct adjustment set follows from the role each node plays, not from how strongly it predicts the outcome.

**Ask students**

Choose the adjustment set before we run the animation. Which node belongs in it, and which two do not?

**Teaching detail**

This is the graded combination of all three stories from this one running example: Family SES & ability (confounder, top), Professional network (mediator, middle), Included in dataset (collider, bottom). Have students decide the full control set before clicking anything, then test it. Correct answer: control for Family SES & ability only. Controlling for Professional network blocks part of the real effect (overcontrol); restricting to cases selected through the two-list rule conditions on the collider and creates selection bias. This is a rehearsal for Parts 3 and 4: in a few minutes you will do exactly this with a real published DAG, except nobody will score it for you — you will have to argue for your own control set.

### Slide 15: What if we prevent confounding before it starts?

**Talk track**

So far we have treated confounding as an analysis problem: find the common cause and adjust for it. Experiments make a stronger move. They change how treatment is assigned so the confounding path is broken before the outcome is measured.

**Teaching detail**

Short transition slide. Everything today, from the first college-and-income widget through the social-media capstone, has been a version of the same move: find the confounder, measure it, control for it. That move needs the confounder to be known and measurable. Twins, adoption, and lotteries — on the next slide — sidestep measurement entirely by changing the design so the back door does not exist, rather than finding and adjusting for it. Druckman's vocabulary, starting after that, gives us a precise way to talk about exactly what that kind of design buys you, and exactly what it still leaves unresolved.

### Slide 16: Design can close paths before analysis

**Talk track**

Twin comparisons, adoption designs, and lotteries all try to build a credible counterfactual into the design. They do it in different ways, but the common goal is to make the treated and untreated comparison informative without measuring every possible common cause.

**Teaching detail**

This is the answer to the question the previous slide just asked. Twins and adoption are the "scientific solution" to the Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference in Druckman's terms, which we name properly starting next slide. Lotteries and natural experiments are the "statistical solution." Correll and Craig & Richeson both build their own lotteries by hand, inside a lab or a survey, rather than finding one in the world — that's exactly what Parts 3 and 4 are about to show in full.

### Slide 17: Experiments close paths by design

**Talk track**

We now have the question for this section: what makes an intervention capable of resolving a causal comparison? Druckman gives us a vocabulary for answering that question precisely.

**Teaching detail**

Open Part 2. Everything in this part comes from Druckman (2023), chapters 2 and 3. The goal is a vocabulary precise enough that students can narrate Parts 3 and 4 themselves, in Druckman's terms, before we even get there.

### Slide 18: We never observe both outcomes for the same unit

**Talk track**

For any one person, we can observe the outcome under treatment or the outcome without treatment, never both at the same moment. The unobserved outcome is the counterfactual. Every causal design is a strategy for replacing that missing comparison.

**Ask students**

For this student, which potential outcome is missing? What real comparison could stand in for it?

**Teaching detail**

This is Holland's Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference, and it is the same idea Week 10 built with the Body Vibes table: for each unit, one potential outcome is necessarily missing. Ask students what comparison they would actually make—this student versus someone else—and what assumption would make that substitute credible. Druckman uses this fact as the foundation for defining an experiment.

### Slide 19: Two ways to construct the missing comparison

**Talk track**

One solution assumes two units are equivalent in every relevant respect except treatment. The other uses random assignment across many units so differences are balanced in expectation. Druckman calls these the scientific and statistical solutions.

**Teaching detail**

Define unit homogeneity precisely before moving on: it is the assumption that two different units — or the same unit at two different points in time — are equivalent in every relevant respect except whether they received the treatment. If that assumption holds, comparing the treated unit to the "identical" untreated one stands in for the impossible comparison of one unit's two potential outcomes.

Why does Druckman call this the *scientific* solution rather than, say, the "assumption-based" solution? Because it is the classic move of the natural sciences, especially chemistry and physics, where a researcher assumes two samples of the same substance — two beakers of water, two bars of the same metal — are interchangeable, so treating one and not the other isolates the treatment's effect without needing any randomization or any large sample at all. It is "scientific" in the sense of being the textbook natural-science method, not in the sense of being more rigorous than the statistical solution — both are equally legitimate ways of resolving the Fundamental Problem, they just substitute different assumptions (homogeneity vs. randomization-produced balance).

Name which of last week's "control by design" fixes used which solution. Twin studies and adoption assume two units (or genomes) are close enough to interchangeable that comparing them stands in for comparing one unit's two worlds — the scientific solution, resting on unit homogeneity. Lotteries and randomized assignment use many units and let randomization do the balancing on average — the statistical solution. Both are legitimate; they just make different assumptions, and a DAG forces you to say which one you're relying on.

### Slide 20: An intervention is what makes a study an experiment

**Talk track**

Druckman defines an experiment by the role of an intervention, not only by whether a researcher personally flips a coin. The intervention must provide the main procedure for resolving the missing counterfactual comparison.

**Teaching detail**

This is deliberately more inclusive than definitions that require random assignment (e.g., Gerber and Green) or researcher control (Morton and Williams). Under this definition, a well-argued natural experiment can count as an experiment even without true randomization, as long as the researcher is using some intervention — researcher-caused or natural — to resolve the Fundamental Problem. Hold this definition loosely for now; the next slide turns it into a typology you can place any study on.

### Slide 21: Four ways an intervention can create a comparison

**Talk track**

Read this table by rows and then columns. The rows ask where the intervention came from. The columns ask whether the causal comparison rests on randomization across many units or on an argument that units are sufficiently homogeneous.

**Ask students**

Where would you place a randomized platform rollout? Where would you place a carefully matched natural comparison?

**Teaching detail**

Rows: source of intervention (researcher-caused vs. natural). Columns: Holland's two solutions (statistical vs. scientific). Cell 1 is ordinary randomized experiments; cell 2 is researcher-caused scientific-solution designs (within-subject, counterbalanced); cell 3 is true random-assignment natural experiments (lotteries nature hands you); cell 4 is "as-if" natural experiments resting on an argued case for unit homogeneity, not actual randomness. Preview: Correll's lab and field studies sit in cell 1. Craig and Richeson's Study 1 is an opportunistic, researcher-caused, statistical-solution design built into an existing survey — still cell 1, just repurposed rather than purpose-built.

Walk through all four cells with one running domain so the 2×2 logic lands as a single coherent story rather than four unrelated examples — same question throughout: does social media use affect depression?

**Cell 1 (researcher-caused, statistical).** A classic randomized experiment: recruit a large sample of social media users, randomly assign half to deactivate their accounts for several weeks and half to continue as normal (this is essentially Allcott, Braghieri, Eichmeyer, and Gentzkow's 2020 Facebook deactivation design from Week 10), then compare depression symptoms between groups at the end. Many units, randomized — the statistical solution doing the work.

**Cell 2 (researcher-caused, scientific).** Same researcher, same intervention, but now resolving the Fundamental Problem with unit homogeneity instead of randomization across many people: a within-subject diary study where each participant gets a researcher-assigned high-use week and a researcher-assigned low-use week, in counterbalanced order, and you compare each person's own mood across their two weeks. The "two units" being compared are the same person at two different times, assumed stable in everything except how much they used social media that week — the scientific solution, still researcher-caused.

**Cell 3 (natural, statistical).** The researcher didn't design the randomization, but it's still genuinely random: a platform rolls out an algorithm change to a random subset of users for engineering/server-load reasons that have nothing to do with mental health, and a researcher later obtains the exposure data and compares depression outcomes between the randomly-exposed and not-yet-exposed groups. Natural source, but still the statistical solution, because the assignment really was random — just not by the researcher's hand.

**Cell 4 (natural, scientific).** No randomization at all, only an argued case for comparability: two adjacent, demographically similar school districts got broadband internet access — and with it, heavy social media use — at different times, purely because of which utility company served each area, unrelated to anything about the students. A researcher comparing depression rates across the two districts has to argue, not assume, that they were otherwise alike (this is structurally identical to the TV-rollout and Sesame Street/broadband examples from Week 10 and from Part 4's discussion) — "as-if" randomization, resting entirely on unit homogeneity the researcher must defend, not statistics.

Close by naming the pattern: moving down the rows (researcher-caused → natural) trades design control for opportunism; moving across the columns (statistical → scientific) trades sample size for an assumption about comparability. Every one of today's four cells asked the exact same substantive question — only the source of the intervention and the logical solution to the Fundamental Problem changed.

Now weigh the four cells against each other — this is the part students actually need for choosing a design, not just naming one.

**Cell 1 (researcher-caused, statistical).** Advantages: the cleanest internal validity of the four — random assignment balances both the confounders you thought of and the ones you didn't, on average; fully replicable; scales to whatever precision a bigger sample buys. Disadvantages: deactivating real people's accounts for weeks is expensive, slow to recruit at scale, and ethically and practically limited (you can't randomly assign someone to heavy use for years); demand effects and attrition are live risks precisely because you're manipulating real behavior among real, socially connected people — which is exactly what makes SUTVA and exclusion violations, two slides from now, a real threat here and not just a textbook worry.

**Cell 2 (researcher-caused, scientific).** Advantages: needs far fewer participants, since every person serves as their own control; removes *all* stable between-person confounders by design, not just the measured ones; good for isolating a mechanism. Disadvantages: assumes temporal stability and no carryover — often implausible for a "sticky" habit like social media use (a low-use week right after a high-use week isn't the same as a low-use week on its own); can't study anything with irreversible or slow-building effects; typically small, unusual samples willing to tolerate a demanding repeated-measures protocol, which costs external validity.

**Cell 3 (natural, statistical).** Advantages: real randomization you didn't have to design, justify to an IRB, or pay for; often large-N and drawn from real platform behavior rather than an artificial manipulation, which buys real-world external validity cell 1 struggles with. Disadvantages: zero control over what got randomized or how, so you're stuck studying whatever variation happened to occur; the "natural" randomization usually bundles several things together (an algorithm change rarely moves just one variable), which is exactly an exclusion-restriction risk; data access and platform cooperation are often the real bottleneck, not the randomization itself.

**Cell 4 (natural, scientific).** Advantages: the only cell that can study big, slow-moving, real-world phenomena that could never be ethically or practically randomized at all, such as a region-wide technology rollout over years; real stakes, real settings. Disadvantages: this is the weakest identification of the four cells — unit homogeneity is an assumption the researcher must argue for, not something guaranteed by design or luck, and it's the one most vulnerable to a confounder hiding in whatever determined the "natural" variation (here, whichever factor decided which district got broadband first). Usually convincing only when triangulated with other designs, not on its own — which is the same lesson Rohrer gave us for DAGs generally: state the assumption, and don't rely on just one design to carry the whole claim.

### Slide 22: Randomization solves one problem, not every problem

**Talk track**

Random assignment gives us independence between assignment and potential outcomes. It does not guarantee that participants receive only one well-defined treatment, that people do not affect one another, or that assignment reaches the outcome through only the intended channel.

**Ask students**

Which of these assumptions is guaranteed by a correctly executed random assignment, and which must still be argued?

**Teaching detail**

Define all three precisely, then use the next three DAGs to show exactly how each failure changes the causal structure.

**Independence** (sometimes called ignorability or unconfoundedness): treatment assignment T is statistically unrelated to the potential outcomes Y₁ and Y₀. True random assignment, correctly executed, guarantees this by construction — it's the one of the three that randomization itself actually buys you for free.

**SUTVA**, the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (Rubin 1980), has two parts, and both get lost if you only remember "no interference": (1) no interference between units — one unit's outcome depends only on its *own* treatment assignment, not on what anyone else was assigned; and (2) no hidden variation of treatment — "deactivate your account" has to mean the same intervention for everyone, not a different experience depending on who delivers it or how. Unlike independence, SUTVA is not automatically guaranteed by randomizing — it's an assumption about the *world*, not about your assignment procedure, and it can fail even when the coin flip was perfectly fair.

**Exclusion restriction** matters most when assignment is used as an instrument for treatment receipt: assignment must affect the outcome only by changing receipt, not through a second channel. For an intent-to-treat effect of assignment itself, that second channel is part of the treatment package rather than a violation of the assignment effect.

The key line is the one worth dwelling on: students' first instinct is that "we randomized, so we're fine." Randomization buys independence. It buys nothing at all about the other two — those have to be argued for, the same way a DAG's assumptions have to be argued for.

### Slide 23: Independence: when compliance reintroduces a confound

**Talk track**

The coin flip randomized the instruction, not what people ultimately did. If we compare people by actual compliance, motivation and self-control can again affect both treatment receipt and the outcome. The confounding problem has returned downstream of assignment.

**Ask students**

Why does analyzing people by what they actually did undo the protection of the original randomization?

**Teaching detail**

Concrete failure, and a very common one: in the deactivation study, random assignment (told to deactivate or not) is clean — but not everyone complies. Some assigned to deactivate don't; some assigned to continue deactivate anyway. If a researcher is tempted to analyze the data by *actual* deactivation status rather than by original assignment — a "per-protocol" or "as-treated" comparison instead of intent-to-treat — independence is gone. Why: self-control and motivation plausibly predict *both* whether someone actually complies with a demanding instruction like "stay off your phone for a month" *and* depression on their own, directly. Compliance is not randomly assigned; only the original instruction was. The dashed arrow from "actually deactivated" to depression is exactly the same fork problem from Part 1, just one step downstream of the coin flip.

This is the single most common way independence quietly breaks in a real randomized experiment, and it is why "intent-to-treat" (analyze by original assignment, regardless of compliance) is the default standard, not a technicality: comparing by assignment preserves the random split; comparing by actual behavior reintroduces exactly the self-selection problem randomization was supposed to kill.

Fixes: report intent-to-treat as the headline estimate; if the compliance-only effect matters, use an instrumental-variables / local-average-treatment-effect approach that uses assignment to instrument for actual compliance, rather than comparing compliers to non-compliers directly; measure and report the compliance rate itself, since a low compliance rate changes how much an ITT null result tells you.

### Slide 24: SUTVA: when units interfere with each other

**Talk track**

SUTVA fails when one person’s treatment changes another person’s outcome, or when the treatment has hidden versions. In this example, B’s outcome depends partly on A’s assignment, so B no longer has a single outcome determined only by B’s own condition.

**Ask students**

What treatment of A could plausibly change B’s outcome in your own research area?

**Teaching detail**

This is Week 10's running-example worked case again, now with a face: A and B are friends in the same study. A, assigned to deactivate, texts B constantly about how much better they feel — B's mood (the outcome) is now partly a function of *A's* treatment assignment, not only B's own. The arrow that shouldn't exist, A's use → B's depression, is drawn in red specifically because it crosses between units, which is the signature of a SUTVA violation: it's not about what causes what *within* a unit, it's about contamination *between* units.

This is also why field experiments on socially connected populations (classrooms, friend networks, platforms) are harder than they look: the more realistic and socially embedded the setting, the more plausible interference becomes. Note the second half of SUTVA too, hidden variation of treatment: if "deactivation" meant something different for teenagers forced off by a parent versus adults who chose it themselves, that's also a SUTVA violation, with no cross-unit arrow needed at all — just two silently different versions of the same labeled treatment.

Fixes: randomize at the cluster level instead of the individual level (whole friend groups, whole schools) so contamination happens within an arm rather than across arms; measure and model exposure to treated peers directly; standardize delivery of the treatment so there's only one version of it.

### Slide 25: Exclusion restriction: when assignment leaks another way

**Talk track**

Exclusion asks whether assignment affects the outcome only through treatment receipt. If assignment also changes awareness, expectations, or reporting, the second path makes the assignment a bundle of interventions rather than a clean lever on use.

**Ask students**

What second pathway from assignment to outcome could exist even if treatment receipt were measured perfectly?

**Teaching detail**

In the deactivation study, assignment is supposed to affect depression only by changing how much people actually use social media. But participants assigned to deactivate may simply *know* they're in the deactivation arm of a study about social media and mental health — that awareness alone (demand effects, a sense of being watched, motivation to report feeling better) could move their mood, entirely independent of whether their use actually changed. The red path, assignment → awareness → depression, is the illegitimate second channel; the blue path, assignment → actual use → depression, is the one the study claims to be isolating.

This is the sharpest of the three to teach because it is the one most students have never had named for them, even though they've felt its cousin: a bad survey-experiment vignette that's so obviously about "the thing researchers are testing" that respondents react to the test, not the treatment.

Fixes: blinding, where feasible (hard here, since people obviously know whether their own account is deactivated); an attention/placebo-matched control condition so both arms feel equally "watched"; measuring actual treatment receipt/compliance so you can separate intent-to-treat from the compliance-only effect; asking directly, post-study, whether participants guessed the hypothesis, and checking whether that guess predicts the outcome.

### Slide 26: Assignment, sampling, and sample size solve different problems

**Talk track**

Random assignment, random sampling, and sample size do different jobs. Assignment supports the internal causal comparison, sampling or population coverage supports generalization, and sample size improves precision and chance balance. None can substitute for the others.

**Ask students**

If I randomly assign 100 undergraduates, which problem have I solved and which problem have I not solved?

**Teaching detail**

This distinction is essential before moving into validity. Random assignment does not guarantee exact covariate balance in a finite sample; it makes imbalance a matter of chance and supports randomization-based uncertainty. Larger samples make severe chance imbalance less likely and standard errors smaller. Random sampling is a different operation entirely and is not required for internal validity, but it can support descriptive representativeness and population generalization.

Use Correll as the preview: undergraduates can be randomly assigned applicant profiles, yielding a strong causal comparison inside the study, while the sample still leaves a generalization question about real hiring managers. Study 2 changes the setting and decision-makers rather than retroactively improving Study 1's random assignment.

### Slide 27: Lab, survey, and field describe where treatment happens

**Talk track**

Lab, survey, and field experiments are labels for where and how the intervention occurs. They do not tell us by themselves whether the causal comparison is strong. A single paper can use more than one setting to answer different validity questions.

**Teaching detail**

Place both upcoming cases on this axis before we get to them in detail, so students have the vocabulary ready. Note that a single paper can use more than one type — Correll's two studies deliberately trade lab control for field realism, which is itself a design choice we'll come back to.

### Slide 28: Experiments can test effects, mechanisms, or policies

**Talk track**

An experiment can establish that an effect exists, test the mechanism producing it, or estimate what a real policy will do. The goal determines how much realism, precision, and contextual similarity the design needs.

**Ask students**

Are the two papers today trying mainly to establish an effect, identify a mechanism, or forecast a policy effect?

**Teaching detail**

Ask: which goal are Correll and Craig & Richeson each pursuing? Both are squarely "searching for facts" — they want to know whether status-based discrimination and status threat exist and operate through the mechanisms claimed, not to hand a policymaker a precise coefficient. This matters later, when we discuss what their modest effect sizes do and don't tell us.

### Slide 29: An artificial setting can still test a theory well

**Talk track**

An experiment can look unlike ordinary life and still isolate the theoretical variable cleanly. Surface realism matters less for a mechanism test than whether participants engage with the task and whether the treatment moves the construct the theory names.

**Ask students**

Can you think of an artificial experiment that still isolates the theoretical mechanism better than a realistic one?

**Teaching detail**

Druckman's claim, following Mook and Plott: experiments are built to isolate a cause by stripping away real-world noise, so demanding that they "look like real life" is often a category error, except specifically for policy-simulation experiments.

Spell out *why*, not just the conclusion. An experiment's whole job is to take one variable, hold everything else constant, and see what moves. Real life never does you that favor — in the real world, the cause you care about always arrives bundled with a dozen other things. So an experiment that strips all of that away and leaves a stylized, artificial-looking setup isn't failing at realism; it's doing exactly the one thing an experiment is for. Plott's line, which is worth putting on the screen: "[The] experiment should be judged by the lessons it teaches about the theory and not by its similarity with what nature might have happened to have created" (Plott 1991: 906). Mundane realism is a claim about the *surface* of the study; what actually licenses a causal inference is whether the manipulation captures the *theoretical construct* — which is a claim about its *depth*. Those can come apart completely, in either direction: a study can look exactly like real life and still manipulate the wrong thing, or look nothing like real life and manipulate exactly the right thing.

Worked example, and genuinely the most persuasive one in the literature for students who are skeptical: Lupia and McCubbins (1998) wanted to test whether people with little information can still make good decisions by using cues about a source's knowledge and whether that source's interests align with their own — a theory about political persuasion and low-information reasoning. Instead of anything that looks like politics, their experiment has participants try to predict the outcome of a coin toss, after hearing from a source who is either knowledgeable-and-biased or unbiased-but-ignorant about how the coin is weighted. There are no candidates, no issues, no campaign ads, nothing a skeptic would call mundane realism at all. But the coin-toss game isolates exactly the theoretical ingredients the theory is about — source expertise and source interest-alignment — with a precision no real political survey item could match, because in a real survey those two things are always tangled up with partisanship, media diet, and a dozen other correlated variables. Ask students: does this experiment tell us anything about politics? Druckman's answer is yes, more cleanly than a "realistic" study would, because it isolates the mechanism the theory claims is doing the work.

Second, shorter anchor, from Mutz (2021: 220), worth reading aloud: "It is not necessary that people in the real world frequently encounter [the] treatment or experience... What is most important about a treatment is that it systematically and substantially changes the independent variable in the intended direction." A treatment doesn't need to be common, or familiar, or something anyone would actually encounter outside a lab — it needs to move the construct, cleanly and substantially, in the direction the theory predicts.

Name the one real exception explicitly, so students don't overgeneralize: Roth's "whispering in the ears of princes" goal from Part 2. If you're trying to tell a policymaker how big an effect to expect from an actual policy, the dosage, framing, and context of your treatment *do* need to resemble the real intervention, because you're no longer just testing whether a mechanism exists — you're trying to forecast a real-world number. Mundane realism becomes load-bearing exactly when the goal shifts from theory-testing to policy simulation, and not before.

Preview the contrast we are about to see in Parts 3 and 4: Correll builds an elaborate, deceptive cover story (a real $135–180K marketing job, full debriefing) that happens to have fairly high mundane realism too — but that's a bonus, not the reason it works. Craig and Richeson use a brief, plain press-release vignette with essentially no mundane realism at all — nothing like how people actually encounter demographic-change news, repeated and politically coded, over months. Both are defensible by Druckman's standard as long as each manipulation is engaging enough that participants take it seriously (experimental realism) and each one moves the actual construct the theory is about (status-threat perception, parental-status salience) — which is precisely what their manipulation checks exist to verify, two slides from now.

### Slide 30: Did the treatment move the intended construct?

**Talk track**

A manipulation check asks whether the intervention changed the intended construct. Attention and comprehension are not enough: participants may understand a message without experiencing the status threat or other psychological state the theory requires.

**Ask students**

What evidence would show that participants understood a treatment but did not experience the intended construct?

**Teaching detail**

A manipulation check is not optional bookkeeping—it is evidence about what the treatment changed. Keep this generic here so the Craig and Richeson result is not revealed before the case. Also distinguish comprehension and attention checks from construct checks: someone can read the article correctly without experiencing the theorized status threat. A manipulation check can itself prime participants if administered before the outcome, so timing matters.

### Slide 31: Every experiment must answer four validity questions

**Talk track**

Use these as four separate questions. Is the statistical relationship credible? Is it causal inside the study? Do the treatment and outcome represent the intended concepts? And can the finding travel to the people, settings, and treatments we care about?

**Ask students**

Which validity question is strongest in a randomized convenience sample, and which remains most debatable?

**Teaching detail**

Four types: statistical conclusion (is the inference from the data to a relationship sound?), internal (is the relationship causal within the study?), construct (does the manipulation/measure capture the intended concept?), and external (does the finding generalize?). We'll anchor each of the first three against Correll and Craig & Richeson in Parts 3–4. The next two slides handle external validity on its own, since it gets the most space in Druckman's chapter 3.

### Slide 32: External validity depends on where effects differ

**Talk track**

A sample is not externally valid or invalid in the abstract. The important question is whether the treatment effect changes across characteristics that the sample does not adequately cover.

**Teaching detail**

Do not re-teach M-STOUT or Henrich et al. here — name them, confirm students remember the acronym and its point, and move straight to what Druckman adds. The sharper claim is coming on the next slide: whether a nonrepresentative sample threatens generalizability is not a fact about the sample's demographics; it's a fact about whether the treatment effect varies by some moderator the sample lacks variance on.

### Slide 33: Generalization requires coverage of relevant moderators

**Talk track**

If the effect is homogeneous, an internally valid estimate may travel widely. If it varies, we need data across the relevant moderator and a way to transport those conditional effects. Without overlap, the target effect is not identified from this sample alone.

**Ask students**

Name one plausible moderator that the Correll undergraduate sample may not cover adequately.

**Teaching detail**

Apply it live to both upcoming cases. Correll's lab sample is undergraduates, not real hiring managers. Prior comparisons suggest student and manager judgments can track similarly, but that is evidence about one possible moderator—not proof that the student estimate transports to every occupation or employer. The field audit supplies new data from the target setting rather than relying entirely on extrapolation.

Craig and Richeson's Studies 3a/3b use heavily male, young MTurk samples. Gender and age are plausible moderators, and the samples provide little coverage for women. Even if both groups are present, merely having some variance is insufficient: conditional effects must be estimated with adequate precision and combined using the target population's composition. When overlap is poor, new data are preferable to heroic extrapolation.

### Slide 34: Two papers use randomization in different ways

**Talk track**

We now have enough vocabulary to read the two papers as design arguments. For each one, we will begin with the observational puzzle, draw the rival causal stories, design an intervention, and then ask what the experiment still cannot establish.

**Teaching detail**

Set expectations for Parts 3 and 4 explicitly: you will be asked to draw, to propose a design, and to criticize a design before seeing the published answer, every single time. Two papers, same throughline, same five moves.

### Slide 35: Correll, Benard & Paik — the motherhood penalty

**Talk track**

Our first case is the motherhood penalty. The paper asks whether mothers are evaluated differently even when employers receive the same evidence about their qualifications and past performance.

**Teaching detail**

Open Part 3. Correll, Benard, and Paik (2007), "Getting a Job: Is There a Motherhood Penalty?," American Journal of Sociology.

### Slide 36: Parenthood and wages are associated, but why?

**Talk track**

Mothers earn less than otherwise comparable childless women, but the wage gap alone cannot tell us why. It could reflect differences in experience or job sorting, discrimination in evaluation, or several mechanisms operating together.

**Ask students**

What evidence would make you interpret the wage gap as discrimination rather than productivity differences?

**Teaching detail**

Set the real-world stakes before any design talk. Ask: what would it take to believe this gap reflects discrimination rather than mothers simply being, on average, less productive at work (shorter tenure, interrupted histories, choice of "mother-friendly" jobs)? That ambiguity is exactly the puzzle the paper is built to resolve.

### Slide 37: The experiment tests a narrower causal effect

**Talk track**

The experiment cannot estimate the total effect of having children on lifetime earnings. It can estimate something narrower and cleaner: the effect of signaling parenthood on the evaluation of an otherwise equivalent applicant.

**Teaching detail**

Make the estimand change explicit. The real-world wage gap motivates the study, but the experiment does not randomly assign women to have children and then observe lifetime earnings. It randomizes whether an applicant profile signals parenthood while holding the documented employment record fixed. The resulting effect is the causal effect of the motherhood cue on judgments and callbacks under those profile conditions.

This is a narrower claim, but it is exactly the piece the survey literature could not isolate. It establishes that unequal treatment can generate part of the motherhood penalty; it does not estimate how much of the population wage gap is due to discrimination versus employment interruptions, occupational sorting, preferences, childcare constraints, or other mechanisms.

### Slide 38: What could produce the motherhood penalty?

**Talk track**

Before seeing the authors’ design, build the causal story. Think separately about common causes of parenthood and wages, consequences of parenthood that may mediate the wage effect, and employer reactions to a motherhood signal.

**Ask students**

Give me one confounder, one mediator, and one employer-evaluation pathway.

**Teaching detail**

Two boxes only: **Motherhood** and **Wages**. What belongs between them, and what kind of node is it?

Do not reveal the DAG image yet. Ask students for at least three kinds of paths rather than forcing every human-capital variable into one role: (1) pre-existing preferences, constraints, ability, and career orientation can affect both parenthood and earnings — confounding; (2) motherhood can change tenure, hours, work interruptions, or occupational sorting — mediation; and (3) a motherhood signal can change employer evaluation — discrimination, also a mediator of the broader wage effect. The point is precisely that "human capital" is not one clean control variable. Its role depends on when and how it is measured.

### Slide 39: Productivity is the central rival explanation

**Talk track**

The rival explanation the experiment is designed to defeat is actual productivity. In observational data, productivity or human capital can influence both parental status patterns and wages. Equal application files remove that source of ambiguity from the comparison.

**Teaching detail**

Reveal the finished DAG and compare to what the class built. Be explicit that this picture isolates only the **pre-treatment confounding channel**: productivity/human capital measured before parenthood. It is not a complete causal model of the motherhood wage penalty.

Some variables commonly entered as controls — continuous work history, tenure, uninterrupted employment — are consequences of motherhood and therefore mediators. Controlling for them removes part of the total effect. Survey data struggle because pre-existing differences and post-parenthood mechanisms are bundled under the same loose label. Correll's experiment sidesteps that ambiguity by holding the entire documented record fixed and randomizing only the cue.

### Slide 40: Motherhood may change the standard used to judge competence

**Talk track**

Status characteristics theory predicts more than a negative stereotype. Once motherhood becomes salient, evaluators may expect lower competence and require stronger evidence before judging a mother to be capable or committed.

**Teaching detail**

This is the competing "discrimination explanation." Status characteristics theory says motherhood functions as a status characteristic in work settings: once salient, it shifts performance expectations and, crucially, the evidentiary bar required to be judged competent, not just the average expectation. This is distinct from simple stereotyping — it's specifically about task-relevant performance expectations and double standards.

### Slide 41: Equal résumés separate two explanations

**Talk track**

Statistical discrimination should disappear when evaluators have complete and equal individual information. Status-based discrimination predicts that the parent label will still change judgments. Equal résumés let the study separate those explanations.

**Ask students**

If two résumés contain equally strong productivity information, what different prediction does each theory make?

**Teaching detail**

Statistical discrimination (left) predicts the gap vanishes once information about individual productivity is complete and equal — a rational employer using group averages only because better information isn't available. Status-based discrimination (right) predicts a direct, independent effect of the label on evaluation, even when productivity is held completely equal. Ask students which DAG the study needs to hold productivity "equal" (conditioned, shown in gold) to distinguish — the answer is both, simultaneously, which is exactly what an experiment can do that a survey cannot.

### Slide 42: How would you isolate discrimination?

**Talk track**

Imagine you have to test this claim without assigning anyone to become a parent. Your intervention has to preserve qualifications and past performance while changing only the information that signals parental status.

**Ask students**

What exactly would you hold fixed, and what single cue would you vary?

**Teaching detail**

Give pairs two to three minutes before revealing Study 1's actual design on the next slide. Push toward: hold everything about a candidate's actual qualifications and performance history completely fixed, and vary only whether they are labeled a parent. If students get there, congratulate them — they've just independently derived the lab study's logic.

### Slide 43: Study 1: what varied within and between participants?

**Talk track**

This is a mixed design. Each participant compares a parent and a nonparent of the same applicant gender and race. Across participants, applicant gender and race vary through random assignment to one of four pair types.

**Ask students**

Which factor varies within a participant, which vary between participants, and which participant characteristic is not randomized?

**Teaching detail**

Explain the mixed design carefully. Each participant evaluated a parent and a nonparent who had the same applicant gender and race, so those attributes were fixed *within that participant's comparison*. But participants were randomly assigned to one of four applicant-pair conditions: African American men, African American women, White men, or White women. Applicant gender and race therefore varied *between participants*. Parental status varied within participants and was counterbalanced across résumé templates; presentation order was counterbalanced too. Participant gender was measured, not randomized.

This matters for the estimand. The cleanest within-participant causal contrast is parent versus nonparent within a given applicant gender/race condition. Comparing the size of that contrast across male and female applicant conditions tests whether parenthood operates differently by applicant gender—the motherhood-penalty interaction.

### Slide 44: Study 1: what did participants actually do?

**Talk track**

Participants believed they were advising a real company about two applicants for a senior marketing job. The outcomes move from beliefs, to the standards applicants must meet, to consequential recommendations about salary, hiring, and promotion.

**Teaching detail**

Make the procedure concrete. Participants believed they were providing real input to a California start-up and were fully debriefed afterward. Each participant compared a parent and nonparent of the same race and gender. The outcome families map directly onto status-characteristics theory: beliefs capture performance expectations; standards capture the double-standard proposition; decisions capture consequential recommendations.

The participant sample is a deliberate vulnerability, not a hidden detail. The authors cite evidence that student and manager evaluations often track similarly, but Study 2 exists partly because that defense is not enough on its own.

### Slide 45: The experiment identifies a cue effect, not the total wage penalty

**Talk track**

The clean causal claim is about a parent cue attached to an application file. It is not a claim that every difference between mothers and nonmothers is discrimination, and it does not estimate the contribution of discrimination to the full population wage gap.

**Teaching detail**

This is the payoff of the earlier estimand slide. The randomized treatment is the parent signal attached to an applicant file. It is not biological or lived parenthood. The study therefore cleanly demonstrates differential treatment of otherwise identical profiles, but it cannot decompose the overall population wage gap or represent every way parenthood changes careers.

Add one nuance to the statistical-versus-status discrimination contrast. Equal résumés rule out actual differences in the applicants' documented past qualifications. An evaluator could still interpret the parent cue as information about future availability. The double-standard outcomes and competence/commitment pattern are evidence for status theory, but the label "status-based" is a theoretical interpretation layered onto the experimentally identified cue effect.

### Slide 46: What could this design still get wrong?

**Talk track**

Internal validity is strong, but that does not make every other concern disappear. Before looking at the results, separate objections about the causal comparison from objections about the participants, occupation, setting, and visibility of the cue.

**Ask students**

Which objection threatens internal validity, and which objection instead concerns construct or external validity?

**Teaching detail**

Let students generate objections: undergraduates aren't real hiring managers; one job type, one high salary band; deception; a single résumé pair per condition. Note which the authors address themselves — they cite Cleveland and Berman (1987) and Olian and Schwab (1988) on student/manager judgment comparability, and the companion field audit study is explicitly designed to answer the "is this just a lab artifact" objection. Which objections survive that defense, and which don't yet have an answer?

### Slide 47: Study 1: the mother cue changed beliefs, standards, and decisions

**Talk track**

Read the rows as a sequence. The mother cue lowers perceived competence, raises the performance threshold required for hire, and changes salary and hiring recommendations. Identical records are being interpreted through different standards.

**Ask students**

Which row is the clearest evidence of a double standard rather than simply a negative rating?

**Teaching detail**

Walk through the four outcomes as a causal sequence rather than asking students to search the published table. The cue changes beliefs about competence, changes the evidentiary standard, and changes consequential recommendations. The required-exam-percentile row is the double standard made concrete: mothers needed a higher score to be judged hirable despite identical actual résumés. Fathers were never penalized, and on several measures were advantaged relative to childless men (higher commitment percentile, more allowed late days, and a higher starting salary). Keep the full published Table 1 available in the reading or notes for students who want every outcome and standard deviation.

### Slide 48: Measured mediation suggests a mechanism but does not identify it

**Talk track**

Competence and commitment statistically account for part of the cue effect, which fits the theory. But those ratings were measured rather than randomized. The mediation result is evidence consistent with the mechanism, not a fully identified causal decomposition.

**Ask students**

What unmeasured variable could affect both competence ratings and hiring recommendations?

**Teaching detail**

Apply the mediation-vs-moderation warning from Part 2 directly. Because competence and commitment are measured rather than randomized, this mediation analysis cannot rule out an unmeasured variable that affects both the mediator and the downstream outcomes. It's suggestive and substantively important — the residual, un-mediated 54–69% is itself a real finding the authors flag honestly — but it is not the same strength of causal claim as what we'll see Craig and Richeson attempt in Part 4.

### Slide 49: The lab result leaves a real-world question

**Talk track**

The lab tells us that the cue can cause discrimination under controlled conditions. It does not tell us whether real employers, making real callback decisions, respond in the same way. That is the question Study 2 is built to answer.

**Ask students**

What does the field audit add that the lab cannot, and what does it give up?

**Teaching detail**

Ask before revealing. The expected answer, in Druckman's terms, is external validity: the lab closes the back door perfectly, but it leaves open whether real institutions, with real stakes and real decision-makers, behave the same way. Study 2 is a field audit study: matched fictitious résumés sent to real employers, with callback as the outcome — the same logic, transplanted into the field.

### Slide 50: An audit moves the same comparison into real hiring

**Talk track**

The audit study sends matched fictitious applications to actual employers. The parent signal varies within a pair, job openings receive a male or female pair, and the behavioral outcome is whether the employer invites the applicant to interview.

**Teaching detail**

Job openings were randomly assigned to receive either a female pair or a male pair, and submission order within pairs was counterbalanced. White-sounding names were used throughout; race was not manipulated in Study 2. The audit preserves the matched-pair intervention while replacing student judgments with real employers and a real behavioral outcome.

It also gives something up. The researchers observe only callback, so they cannot tell whether a real employer inferred lower competence, lower commitment, scheduling difficulty, expected leave, or something else. This is triangulation: Study 1 has stronger measurement of mechanism; Study 2 has stronger realism and consequence.

### Slide 51: Real employers called back mothers less often

**Talk track**

The field result mirrors the lab for women. Childless women received 21 callbacks and mothers received 10 out of the same number of applications. The study observes a consequential decision, although it no longer observes the employer’s reasoning.

**Ask students**

Can callback behavior establish why employers discriminated?

**Teaching detail**

There were 56 callbacks in total. Mothers received 10 callbacks from 320 applications; childless women received 21 from 320. No detectable father bonus appeared in the field, unlike the lab. The audit study cannot say *why* employers discriminate — there is no rating data from real employers — but it establishes that the lab-demonstrated bias translates into a real, consequential labor-market outcome. Note that the low callback count makes subgroup estimates less precise even though the mother/nonmother contrast is statistically significant.

### Slide 52: The field study gains realism but loses the mechanism

**Talk track**

The field study improves realism and changes the decision-maker, but the tradeoff is information about mechanism. A callback tells us that treatment differed; it does not tell us whether the employer inferred lower competence, availability, commitment, or something else.

**Teaching detail**

Ask first, then compare against what the paper itself flags: why employers in the field discriminate is untested (no mechanism data there); the lab's residual 54–69% unmediated effect is unexplained; generalizability beyond one high-status marketing job is untested; and the paper surfaces, but doesn't resolve, an unexplained race-based salary penalty with no corresponding competence/commitment gap — a different discriminatory process the design wasn't built to unpack.

### Slide 53: Randomization severs the productivity path

**Talk track**

Random assignment breaks the link between actual applicant productivity and the assigned parent cue. The applicants’ real qualifications cannot explain why one file receives the parent signal. That is the path the experiment closes by design.

**Ask students**

Point to the path that random assignment breaks. What remains outside the experiment?

**Teaching detail**

Give pairs a minute, then cold-call one to present. The randomization cuts the arrow from actual productivity into the assigned parental-status signal — the back door that made the observational comparison uninterpretable is now structurally closed, not just statistically adjusted for. Actual motherhood was not randomized; the applicant-profile cue was.

### Slide 54: Correll shows what a well-chosen manipulation can isolate

**Talk track**

Correll randomizes an upstream cue and then measures the proposed psychological mechanism. Our next paper pushes one step further by changing the message in a way intended to raise or reduce the proposed mediator itself.

**Teaching detail**

Short bridge. Remind students of the mediation warning from Part 2—Correll's mediation analysis measured competence and commitment rather than manipulating them. The next case shows what it looks like to take that warning seriously and experimentally manipulate the proposed mechanism. Avoid saying the researchers literally assigned each participant a value of experienced threat; they randomized a message designed to raise or assuage it.

### Slide 55: Craig & Richeson — majority-minority status threat

**Talk track**

The second case asks how White Americans respond politically to information that the United States is becoming a majority-minority country. As before, we need to separate the broad social puzzle from the narrower effect the experiments can identify.

**Teaching detail**

Open Part 4. Craig and Richeson (2014, Psychological Science), "On the Precipice of a 'Majority-Minority' America," with the 2015 corrigendum.

### Slide 56: Demographic change correlates with conservatism, but why?

**Talk track**

Places experiencing demographic change have sometimes shown greater White conservatism, but a geographic correlation is compatible with many causal stories. The experiment begins by changing exposure to information rather than changing the population itself.

**Ask students**

What are two explanations for the geographic correlation other than status threat?

**Teaching detail**

This correlational finding motivates the whole paper. It's consistent with a racial-threat story, but it's also consistent with several other structures, which is exactly what the next slide gets students to generate themselves.

### Slide 57: What else could produce this correlation?

**Talk track**

Before accepting the threat explanation, generate alternatives. Conservatism may affect how people notice or interpret demographic change, and regional history or economic conditions may affect both demographic patterns and politics.

**Ask students**

Which arrow could run in the opposite direction? What regional variable could confound the relationship?

**Teaching detail**

Build whichever structures students propose, live. Push toward at least three: reverse causation (already-conservative Whites selectively notice or overreport the demographic shift); a regional confounder (places with faster demographic change may also differ in local economic conditions, urbanicity, or partisan history); and a genuine causal arrow running through perceived status threat. Ask: which structure does Giles and Hertz's correlational data fit, and why can't correlational data alone tell us which one is right?

### Slide 58: One correlation fits three causal stories

**Talk track**

All three diagrams can generate the same observed correlation. The experiment targets the third story by assigning exposure to demographic-shift information while holding actual location and racial composition fixed.

**Teaching detail**

Compare the class's proposals to these three. All three are consistent with a raw correlation between local racial composition and White conservatism. Only an experiment that manipulates exposure to the demographic information directly — holding region, actual local composition, and prior ideology fixed — can adjudicate between them.

### Slide 59: The experiments answer a narrower question

**Talk track**

Keep the estimand narrow. These studies identify the short-term attitudinal effect of seeing a particular message. They do not identify the effect of living through decades of demographic change or repeated partisan coverage on voting behavior.

**Ask students**

What is the treatment here: demographic change itself, or exposure to a message about it?

**Teaching detail**

Make the estimand switch as explicit as it was in Correll. The parish-level correlation motivates the theory, but the experiments manipulate information about demographic change. Their internally valid claim concerns the short-term attitudinal effect of that exposure under the specific survey conditions. They do not identify the effect of a community's actual demographic composition, repeated partisan media coverage, or years of social change on real voting behavior.

### Slide 60: Status threat could connect the message to conservatism

**Talk track**

The proposed chain is that a message about losing numerical majority status creates group-status threat, which then shifts political attitudes in a conservative direction. The mechanism is social and symbolic rather than an immediate physical threat.

**Teaching detail**

The motivated-cognition literature mostly tested mortality salience and terrorism threat. The theoretical contribution here is extending the same logic to a specifically social, zero-sum status threat — the perception that a rising minority share mechanically lowers the in-group's own relative standing — with no proximate physical danger and a multi-decade time horizon.

### Slide 61: What control isolates the majority-status implication?

**Talk track**

A useful control must contain racial-composition information without implying that White majority status is disappearing. That lets the design isolate the status meaning of the message rather than simple exposure to racial news.

**Ask students**

What should the control condition contain, and what should it deliberately omit?

**Teaching detail**

Let pairs propose a control before revealing. The actual Study 1 control: a survey form asking whether respondents had heard that Hispanics and Blacks were roughly equal in number nationally — racial-composition news, but without the majority-status framing. This holds "exposure to racial-composition news in general" constant while varying whether the shift implies a change in who is the numerical majority.

### Slide 62: An old Pew split becomes an experiment

**Talk track**

Study 1 repurposes an existing randomized split in a Pew survey. White independents saw either the majority-minority question or a racial-composition control, and the authors examined party leaning and ideology.

**Teaching detail**

Place this in Druckman's typology: cell 1, researcher-caused and statistical-solution, but opportunistic rather than purpose-built—the randomization already existed in Pew's survey design, and the authors found a use for it years later. The control holds exposure to racial-composition news roughly constant while removing the change-in-majority-status implication. Explain the restriction to political independents: the outcome is party leaning, so committed partisans have less room to move and are less informative about a short-term shift.

### Slide 63: The corrigendum weakens Study 1

**Talk track**

The corrigendum changes how strongly we should describe Study 1. After the weighting error was corrected, the national party-lean result was no longer conventionally significant, ideology did not move, and the West estimate remained imprecise.

**Ask students**

After the correction, what language is justified: strong evidence, suggestive evidence, or no information at all?

**Teaching detail**

Use this as a methods lesson and calibrate the evidence at the same time. This kind of weighting error is a real pitfall with complex survey weights, and a public corrigendum—rather than silence—is the correction system working. But transparency does not restore the original result: the corrected national estimate is inconclusive, general ideology did not move, and the larger West estimate is based on 49 respondents and also falls short of the conventional threshold. The paper's argument must therefore rest on convergence with Studies 2–3, not a decisive Study 1.

### Slide 64: What does Study 1 still leave unresolved?

**Talk track**

Study 1 offers a randomized contrast, but it has weak corrected evidence and no direct test of the proposed mechanism. It also relies on self-reported attitudes from a secondary dataset not designed around the full theory.

**Ask students**

What part of the causal chain has not been measured or manipulated yet?

**Teaching detail**

Push toward: Study 1 has a measured outcome (party lean, ideology) but no mediator at all — no test of *why* the shift would move conservatism; it's a single secondary dataset; and it measures self-reported party lean, not any behavior. All three motivate Study 2's design, which we see next.

### Slide 65: Study 2 builds the experiment the theory needed

**Talk track**

Study 2 is purpose-built. It compares a racial-shift press release with a geographic-mobility control, measures both race-related and race-neutral policy attitudes, and measures several possible psychological mediators.

**Teaching detail**

This is the design information missing from the earlier version. The control matches the broad form of a press release about social change but removes racial content. The focal policy outcomes include three race-related items and two race-neutral items, allowing the authors to ask whether the response is targeted or ideologically broader. The reliability of the two short subscales is modest, which belongs in the later critique.
